body_html:
Meeting your partner’s family in Spanish is one of the most nerve-racking evenings a learner can face. You want to make a good impression, the conversation moves fast, and everyone is curious about you. The good news: families usually care far more about respect and warmth than about perfect grammar. With a few prepared phrases and an understanding of the customs, you can relax and actually enjoy it.

Key takeaways
  • Start with usted for parents and grandparents unless they invite you to use tú.
  • Bring a small gift: dessert, flowers or something from your country.
  • Compliment the food and the home sincerely and often.
  • Prepare a short answer to “How did you two meet?”
{{toc}}

Meeting your partner’s family in Spanish: tú or usted?

This is the first decision. In much of Latin America, using usted with your partner’s parents and grandparents shows respect, especially at a first meeting. In Spain, tú is more common even with in-laws, but starting with usted is never rude. Often the parents will say Tutéame, por favor or Háblame de tú (“Call me tú”), and then you can relax. Ask your partner what their family prefers. It is the single most useful thing you can do before the visit.

Greetings at the door

SpanishEnglish
Mucho gusto.Nice to meet you.
Encantado / Encantada de conocerla.Delighted to meet you (to a woman, usted).
Encantado / Encantada de conocerlo.Delighted to meet you (to a man, usted).
Gracias por recibirme.Thank you for having me.
Les traje un postre.I brought you a dessert.
Qué casa tan bonita.What a lovely home.

Expect a kiss on the cheek (one in most of Latin America, two in Spain) or a warm handshake from older men. Follow their lead.

{{image:2}}

Questions they will ask you

Prepare short, friendly answers to these. You will almost certainly hear them.

  • ¿Cómo se conocieron? How did you meet? → Nos conocimos en el trabajo / en una fiesta / por una aplicación.
  • ¿De dónde eres? Where are you from? → Soy de Canadá, de Toronto.
  • ¿A qué te dedicas? What do you do? → Trabajo como enfermera / Soy ingeniero.
  • ¿Hablas español? Do you speak Spanish? → Un poco. Estoy aprendiendo, ¡tengan paciencia conmigo! (A little. I’m learning, be patient with me!)
  • ¿Te gusta la comida? Do you like the food? → ¡Me encanta! Está riquísima.

Questions you can ask them

Asking questions shows interest and gives you time to listen instead of speak.

  • ¿Cómo era [nombre] de niño / niña? What was [name] like as a child? (Families love this one.)
  • ¿Usted cocinó todo esto? Did you cook all this?
  • ¿Cuánto tiempo llevan viviendo aquí? How long have you lived here?
  • ¿Me enseña la receta algún día? Will you teach me the recipe one day?
{{book:love-slowly}}

At the table

Food is the heart of most family gatherings. Before eating, people often say ¡Buen provecho! or just ¡Provecho! (Enjoy your meal). Useful lines:

  • Todo está delicioso. Everything is delicious.
  • ¿Me pasa el pan, por favor? Could you pass the bread, please? (usted)
  • Sí, un poquito más, gracias. Yes, a little more, thanks.
  • Estoy lleno / llena, pero estaba buenísimo. I’m full, but it was excellent.
  • ¡Salud! Cheers!

Refusing food can be tricky; a second small helping is often appreciated. For more table phrases, see {{link:family-dinner-spanish-phrases|Spanish phrases for family dinner}} and {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}}.

Offering help and good manners

  • ¿Le ayudo con algo? Can I help you with anything?
  • ¿Le ayudo a recoger la mesa? Shall I help clear the table?
  • Con permiso. Excuse me (when leaving the table or passing someone).
  • Perdón, no entendí. ¿Me lo puede repetir? Sorry, I didn’t understand. Could you repeat it?

Offering to help, even if they say no, is noticed and appreciated in almost every Spanish-speaking household.

{{image:3}}

A sample conversation

  • Mother: ¡Bienvenido! Pasa, pasa. ¿Cómo estás? (Welcome! Come in, come in. How are you?)
  • You: Muy bien, gracias. Encantado de conocerla, señora. Le traje unas flores. (Very well, thanks. Lovely to meet you. I brought you some flowers.)
  • Mother: ¡Qué detalle! No te hubieras molestado. (How thoughtful! You shouldn’t have.)
  • Father: Así que tú eres el famoso Daniel. ¿Cómo se conocieron? (So you’re the famous Daniel. How did you meet?)
  • You: En una clase de baile. Ella bailaba muy bien… y yo muy mal. (At a dance class. She danced very well… and I danced very badly.)

A little self-deprecating humor goes a long way. Families relax when they see you are relaxed.

Saying goodbye

  • Muchas gracias por todo. Me sentí como en casa. Thank you so much for everything. I felt at home.
  • La comida estuvo deliciosa. The food was delicious.
  • Espero verlos pronto. I hope to see you soon.

Goodbyes can take a long time; a despedida at the door, and then another by the car, is completely normal.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using tú with grandparents straight away. Wait to be invited.
  • Arriving empty-handed. A small gift matters more than its price.
  • Saying estoy embarazado/a for “I’m embarrassed”. It means pregnant. Say me da vergüenza.
  • Refusing all food. Try a little of everything if you can.

The vocabulary of in-laws is worth knowing too: the RAE dictionary lists suegro and suegra for parents-in-law, and you will hear cuñado and cuñada for siblings-in-law. Continue with {{link:talking-to-your-in-laws-in-spanish|talking to your in-laws in Spanish}}, or explore more situations in {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

Meeting your partner’s family in Spanish is less about speaking perfectly and more about showing that you care: about their child, their food and their language. Arrive with a gift, ask questions, compliment the cook and say thank you twice. That is a recipe that works in any family.

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted with my partner’s parents?
faq.a: In much of Latin America, start with usted as a sign of respect. In Spain tú is more common, but usted is never rude at a first meeting. Switch when they invite you.

faq.q: What gift should I bring when meeting a Spanish-speaking family?
faq.a: A dessert, flowers, a bottle of wine if the family drinks, or a small gift from your home country are all good choices. The gesture matters more than the price.

faq.q: How do I say “nice to meet you” to my girlfriend’s mother?
faq.a: Mucho gusto works everywhere. A warmer option is Encantado de conocerla (said by a man) or Encantada de conocerla (said by a woman).
